title: The workers hired late (Matthew 20:1–16)
hook: those who worked one hour get the same wage as those who worked all day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the son who stayed, standing outside the party. Your line was all I have is yours. Did you catch yourself keeping score? Day forty-nine, the last day of the parables week. It ends with the most unfair story he told.

Dawn in the town square. Men are standing around, waiting to be picked for a day's work, the way day laborers still wait outside hardware stores this morning. A landowner comes and hires some for his vineyard, for the usual day's wage, a denarius. At nine he comes back and hires more. At noon, more. At three, more. And at five in the afternoon, with an hour of daylight left, he finds men still standing there. "Why stand you here all the day idle?" Because no one hired us, they say. Go on, then, he says, into the vineyard. Then evening comes, and it's time to pay. Today: the payday nobody expected.
screen: `DAWN, NINE, NOON, THREE.` → `FIVE O'CLOCK: STILL WAITING.` → `THEN, PAYDAY.`

segments.voice: The landowner tells his steward: pay them, starting with the last ones hired. The five o'clock crew steps up and gets a full denarius. A whole day's wage for one hour. Down the line, the dawn crew is doing the math. If they got a denarius, we're getting a lot more. Then they get a denarius. Exactly what they agreed to. And they grumble. These last worked one hour, and you've made them equal to us, who bore the burden of the day and the heat. It's hard not to agree with them. The landowner answers one of them: friend, I'm doing you no wrong. Didn't you agree to a denarius? Take what's yours and go. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Or, is it not lawful for me to do what I will? is thy eye evil, because I am good?" An evil eye, in that world, meant envy: a look that resents someone else's good luck. The problem isn't that the dawn workers were cheated. They weren't. The problem is that someone else was given a gift. "So shall the last be first, and the first last." The Catholic Church teaches that grace is exactly this: a free gift, undeserved, not wages earned. The Catechism describes it as favor: help from God that is free and undeserved. Nobody clocks in for it. And this week's stories all say it: a sower throwing seed everywhere, a seed and some yeast, a Samaritan stopping, a sheep and a coin found, two sons and a father who runs, and now a payday that makes no sense on a spreadsheet.
screen: `PAY THE LAST ONES FIRST.` · `A FULL DAY'S WAGE FOR ONE HOUR.` · `IS THY EYE EVIL?` · `GRACE: A GIFT, NOT WAGES.` · then, large: `THE LAST SHALL BE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be glad for someone else's gift. Settle and breathe. Think of someone who recently got something good: a raise, a baby, a trip, praise you felt you deserved more. Notice if there's a little sting. That's the evil eye, and everyone has one. Don't scold yourself. Just picture that person's face when they got the good news, and try, for one breath, to be glad with them. If you pray, you can thank God for their gift. The bell holds the time.
The workers hired late. One hour's work, a full day's pay, and the grumbling of those who worked all day. Today's word.
Your line: grace isn't a wage. Today, congratulate someone for a good thing that came to them, and mean it. Day forty-nine. Next week: signs on the road.

howItsDone: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass, and the Catechism teaches that grace is a free and undeserved gift from God; many use the story to examine envy before confession.

original.note: Greek, from Latin denarius: a silver coin, a common day's wage for a laborer.

trapdoor: what you thought: an unfair boss.
what it means: nobody was cheated. the problem is that someone else got a gift. grace isn't wages.
what a scholar hears: the evil eye meant envy. the Catechism defines grace as favor, the free and undeserved help God gives.
